nodes.label: SAM.gov registration
nodes.one_line: Register your entity in SAM.gov with a Unique Entity ID so you can legally apply for and receive federal awards.
know_what: the Unique Entity ID (UEI) — the 12-character SAM.gov identifier that replaced the DUNS number in 2022 and is required on every federal application
the annual renewal requirement — a SAM.gov registration must be revalidated at least once every 12 months or the entity drops to inactive
entity validation — SAM.gov confirms the legal business name and physical address against IRS records (EIN match) before the UEI is issued
Reps & Certs — the representations and certifications (debarment, lobbying, tax) that accompany every registration and flow into applications
active vs inactive status — only an active registration is accepted by Grants.gov; a lapsed one rejects your submission at the portal
2 CFR 25 — the regulation requiring SAM registration as a condition of receiving any federal award or subaward
the free registration fact — GSA never charges for SAM.gov, and third-party sites that bill for 'registration help' are a known scam vector
know_how: register at SAM.gov with an entity administrator account and complete the full entity registration, including the UEI and Reps & Certs
enter the legal business name exactly as it appears on your EIN confirmation from the IRS, or validation fails
renew the registration at least 60 days before the 12-month anniversary, because reactivation after lapse can take 5-10 business days
verify active status on the SAM.gov entity page before starting any federal application, not after drafting
update Reps & Certs whenever entity information (address, officials, NAICS codes) changes, since stale data blocks award acceptance
link the SAM.gov registration to Grants.gov once so the portal pulls your entity profile into every Workspace application
habits: keeping a calendar reminder for SAM renewal set 60 days before the 12-month anniversary, and treating the lapse date as a hard deadline
checking SAM active status at the start of every federal opportunity, before any drafting hours are spent
using the IRS-confirmed legal name on every form, never the operating name, to keep validation clean
billing nothing for registration — flagging any third-party SAM 'service' that asks for payment as a scam
re-running the entity validation check when the IRS EIN or mailing address changes, before it bites a submission
nodes.checkpoint: Register your entity in SAM.gov, confirm the UEI appears in an active registration, and name the displayed 12-month renewal date with a calendar entry set at least 60 days before it.
nodes.common_failure: Letting the registration lapse, so a finished application is rejected at the Grants.gov portal; entering the operating name instead of the IRS legal name and failing entity validation; paying a third-party site for what GSA provides free; starting the registration the week of a deadline when activation can take 5-10 business days.
sources: SAM.gov — GSA entity registration and UEI guidance
2 CFR Part 25 — Universal Identifier & Central Contractor Registration
Grants.gov Learning Center — SAM registration requirements

nodes.label: NOFO deconstruction
nodes.one_line: Extract deadlines, eligibility, page limits, and review criteria from a Notice of Funding Opportunity so you plan the response before writing.
know_what: the NOFO's anatomy — the section-by-section Notice of Funding Opportunity on Grants.gov: agency, Assistance Listing number, eligibility, page limits, review criteria, and submission deadlines
the 5:00 pm ET deadline convention — most federal applications close at 5:00 pm Eastern Time on the due date, regardless of your time zone
review criteria and point weights — the scored sections and their percentages (e.g., approach 30%, need 20%) that the agency will use to rank applications
page limits and formatting rules — narrative caps (e.g., 25 pages), font and margin requirements, and which attachments count against the cap
mandatory vs optional attachments — the difference between forms and documents required for a complete application and those that are voluntary
amendments — agencies revise NOFOs; the revised version and its change history on Grants.gov override anything you drafted against the original
the funding opportunity description (FOD) vs the application guide — the NOFO announces the competition, the agency's application guide carries the mechanics
know_how: read the NOFO twice: once for deadlines and eligibility, once for page limits, review criteria, and attachment requirements
build a one-page compliance sheet listing every deadline, page limit, eligibility condition, and review criterion with its point weight
extract the review criteria into a draft scoring table before writing, so the narrative is structured to answer them
date-stamp the NOFO version you are drafting against and re-check Grants.gov for amendments at least weekly
flag agency-specific requirements (forms, formats, registrations) that differ from the Grants.gov standard
note the Assistance Listing number and search for the program's prior-year NOFO and awarded abstracts to see what scored
habits: producing the compliance sheet before the outline, never after the draft
checking Grants.gov for NOFO amendments on every project team meeting until submission
reading the eligibility and page-limit sections aloud to a second person before committing hours
filing every NOFO version and amendment notice in the opportunity folder so the drafting baseline is provable
re-reading the review criteria immediately before the final revision pass to catch drift from the scoring rubric
nodes.checkpoint: From a real NOFO, produce a one-page compliance sheet naming every deadline, page limit, eligibility condition, and review criterion with its point weight — completed before drafting begins.
nodes.common_failure: Drafting against an amended-out NOFO because the revision was never checked; skipping page-limit details until the final hour; discovering mid-draft that your entity is ineligible; treating a proposal template as the agency's requirements and missing agency-specific forms.
sources: Grants.gov — Understanding the NOFO / funding opportunity resources
NIH — How to Read a Funding Opportunity Announcement (grants.nih.gov)
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need

nodes.label: Deadline discipline
nodes.one_line: Work backward from a hard submission time to a writing and review schedule, and submit with margin instead of in the last hour.
know_what: the 5:00 pm ET cutoff — federal applications close at 5:00 pm Eastern Time on the due date; the portal stops accepting at that instant
the reverse timeline — planning backward from the due date: final review, internal deadline, attachment assembly, and draft milestones
the 24-48 hour margin — the convention of landing the submission at least a full day early, because the portal, not your writing, is the last dependency
Grants.gov Workspace — the online environment where you assemble and test-submit an application before the real deadline
portal maintenance windows — Grants.gov posts scheduled outages; a planned submission during one is a self-inflicted miss
the tracking number — Grants.gov's submission receipt (GRANT number) that proves the application arrived before the cutoff
know_how: build a reverse timeline from the 5:00 pm ET due date: narrative freeze, internal review, attachments, and validation, each with a named owner
set the internal submission deadline 3-5 days before the federal deadline so reviewer feedback has a landing spot
plan to submit at least 24-48 hours before the cutoff, then use the slack for validation-error fixes
test the application in Workspace before the real submission to catch form and attachment problems early
confirm receipt via the Grants.gov tracking number and save the confirmation page and downloaded package
check the Grants.gov system status page before the final submission window and reschedule around announced maintenance
habits: never planning to submit on the due date — treating the internal deadline as the real one
building slack into every milestone, because drafts always slip and the portal never waits
submitting and confirming the tracking number before the final day, never on it
treating Grants.gov downtime as a certainty to plan around, not a risk to accept
keeping the reverse timeline visible on the project tracker so no milestone drifts silently
nodes.checkpoint: Build a reverse timeline for a real NOFO with named internal milestones that lands submission at least 24 hours before the 5:00 pm ET cutoff, and submit a test application to your Grants.gov workspace.
nodes.common_failure: Treating the due date as the submission date, so a single validation error or portal outage becomes a missed deadline; drafting up to the final hour with no review margin; forgetting that 5:00 pm ET is a hard cutoff, not a target window.
sources: Grants.gov — Deadline and system status guidance
Beverly Browning, Grant Writing For Dummies — timeline planning
Carlson & O'Neal-McElrath, Winning Grants Step by Step

nodes.label: Grants.gov submission
nodes.one_line: Assemble and submit an application through Grants.gov — forms, attachments, validation — without tripping the portal's rejections.
know_what: the SF-424 family — the Application for Federal Assistance (SF-424) plus the SF-424A budget form and SF-424B assurances that anchor most federal applications
standard vs agency-specific forms — some competitions replace the standard set with agency forms, and the NOFO's instructions control
Workspace — Grants.gov's online application assembly environment, where you complete forms, attach documents, and validate
validation errors and warnings — hard errors block submission; warnings submit but flag issues; both must be read before the deadline
attachment requirements — PDF format, named files, page limits, and file-size caps (many agencies cap individual attachments at 10 MB)
the tracking number — the GRANT number returned at submission that is your proof the application was received before the cutoff
know_how: build the application in Grants.gov Workspace, completing every required form field with data from a single source of truth
convert attachments to PDF, name them exactly as the NOFO specifies, and verify each is under the agency's page and size caps
run validation the day before submission, fix every error, and review every warning rather than dismissing it
submit at least 24-48 hours before the 5:00 pm ET deadline so validation failures have time to be repaired
save the tracking number and download a copy of the submitted package for the award file
use the Grants.gov help desk and Knowledge Base when a form or validation error is not self-explanatory
habits: running validation the day before submission, never the hour of
keeping attachments under page and file-size limits and re-checking them at assembly, not at draft
reading every validation warning as a question to answer, not a box to ignore
archiving the submitted package, tracking number, and dated confirmation in the opportunity folder
building a reusable checklist of the SF-424 fields your organization always enters, to cut re-entry errors
nodes.checkpoint: Submit a complete application through Grants.gov Workspace that passes validation with zero errors, and capture the tracking number and a downloaded copy of the submitted package.
nodes.common_failure: Fixing validation errors under deadline pressure after the margin was spent; forgetting an attachment until the system lists it missing; uploading a corrupt or oversized PDF that the portal silently rejects; assuming the SF-424 family applies when the agency specified different forms.
sources: Grants.gov — Workspace user guide and How to Apply instructions
Grants.gov — SF-424 forms and instructions
2 CFR 200.313 — Federal financial reporting forms reference

nodes.label: Eligibility check
nodes.one_line: Confirm your entity type, geography, and track record satisfy every threshold before committing hours to an application.
know_what: the eligible-applicant categories — 501(c)(3) nonprofits, units of government (state, local, Tribal), and institutions of higher education, with for-profits excluded from most federal competitions
the NOFO's Eligible Applicants section — the verbatim list of entity types, geographic areas, and track-record conditions that gate entry
geographic eligibility — service-area requirements (e.g., rural counties, specific states) that disqualify otherwise capable applicants
entity-type exclusions — competitions limited to units of government or IHEs where a 501(c)(3) cannot apply at all
applicant-type codes — the standardized categories (e.g., 'A' for nonprofits, '25' for government) agencies use in their forms
eligibility as a precondition — an active SAM registration and, often, a UEI are part of being eligible to apply, not just to receive
know_how: read the NOFO's Eligible Applicants section verbatim and map each condition to your entity's actual status
check the geographic scope against your service area before drafting, not after
confirm the entity type — 501(c)(3) determination letter, unit-of-government status, or IHE accreditation — with the document that proves it
verify prerequisite registrations (SAM active, UEI current) as part of the eligibility determination
document the determination in one line with the NOFO section cited, and re-run it if the NOFO is amended
check whether the competition requires a consortium, partnership, or match as a condition of eligibility, and confirm you can meet it
habits: checking eligibility before writing a word of the narrative, as a binary gate
treating 501(c)(3) status as qualifying for some, not all, competitions
re-verifying eligibility after every NOFO amendment, since criteria change
keeping the IRS determination letter, state registration, and SAM status in one place so the check takes minutes
recording the eligibility determination and its source in the opportunity folder for later auditors and reviewers
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a written eligibility determination for a real NOFO, quoting the exact Eligible Applicants language that admits or excludes your entity, before any drafting hours are spent.
nodes.common_failure: Assuming 501(c)(3) status opens every federal door; missing a unit-of-government or IHE-only restriction until after weeks of drafting; ignoring the geographic service-area condition; treating eligibility as a paperwork detail rather than the first gate.
sources: Grants.gov — Search and eligibility filters documentation
National Council of Nonprofits — federal grants eligibility guidance
IRS — 501(c)(3) determination and public charity status

nodes.label: Award terms review
nodes.one_line: Review the notice of award's terms and conditions and flag anything you cannot commit to before you accept the money.
know_what: the notice of award (NoA) — the document that makes the grant official and carries the terms, period of performance, and budget
2 CFR 200's subparts — Subpart A (definitions), C (pre-award requirements), D (post-award requirements), E (cost principles), and F (audit requirements), which govern federal awards
general vs specific conditions — standard terms that apply to every award plus agency- or award-specific special conditions
the period of performance — the start and end dates within which the money can be spent, and whether extension is possible
payment method — advance payment vs reimbursement, and the cash-flow difference between them for your organization
reporting requirements — the scheduled interim and final reports (financial and narrative) with their due dates
match and cost-share commitments — the matching dollars the award requires you to raise or spend
know_how: read the NoA's terms and conditions in full, including the general terms attached as an appendix, before signing
extract every commitment — period of performance, payment method, match, reporting dates, special conditions — into a one-page terms summary
flag any term the organization cannot commit to (cash-flow, match, staffing, data sharing) and escalate before acceptance
calendar the reporting due dates and the period-of-performance end from the NoA, not from memory
check the award's cost principles under 2 CFR 200 Subpart E for anything that changes how the budget may be spent
confirm the acceptance mechanism and its deadline, since some awards require an explicit acceptance or drawdown setup
habits: reviewing terms before the acceptance deadline, never after spending begins
treating the NoA terms as binding commitments, not boilerplate
putting every reporting date from the NoA on the calendar the day the award arrives
re-reading special conditions when anything about the project changes mid-period
keeping the NoA and terms summary in the award file with the application package
nodes.checkpoint: Review a real notice of award and produce a commitment summary listing the period of performance, payment method, match, and reporting dates, flagging every term the organization cannot accept before signing.
nodes.common_failure: Accepting the award without reading the terms, then discovering a special condition that changes the project; missing a reimbursement-only payment method that the organization cannot cash-flow; treating 2 CFR 200 as uniform and missing the agency's specific conditions.
sources: 2 CFR Part 200 — Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements for Federal Awards
GSA — Federal award terms and conditions template
National Council of Nonprofits — federal award management guidance

nodes.label: Regranting & subawards
nodes.one_line: Pass federal or foundation funds through to subrecipients with written subawards and their own compliance duties.
know_what: the subaward vs contract distinction (2 CFR 200.1) — a subrecipient carries out part of the program and is subject to the award's requirements; a contractor provides goods or services for a fee
the pass-through entity — the recipient that flows funds down and keeps oversight duty under 2 CFR 200 Subpart D
the written subaward — the required agreement naming scope, budget, period, reporting, and audit responsibilities of the subrecipient
flow-down provisions — the federal requirements (2 CFR 200, single-audit, records) that must be passed through in the subaward agreement
subrecipient monitoring — the pass-through entity's duty to review subrecipient reports, expenditures, and performance on a schedule
subrecipient risk assessment — evaluating a subrecipient's financial and management capacity before awarding, per 2 CFR 200.332
foundation and intermediary regranting — private funders and United Ways that pass their own grants down with simpler but still written agreements
know_how: classify each flow-through as subaward or contract using the 2 CFR 200.330 indicators (programmatic responsibility, compliance, contribution to the program)
issue a written subaward for every pass-through, naming scope, approved budget, period of performance, and reporting cadence
run a subrecipient risk assessment before the award and set monitoring intensity accordingly
monitor subrecipients on a published schedule — reports, expenditure review, and site visits — and document each review
flow down the federal requirements the subaward inherits, including 2 CFR 200 and single-audit duties
collect and review the subrecipient's reports before releasing the next drawdown or installment
habits: writing the subaward agreement before passing any money, never after
monitoring on a schedule, not on exception — the first missed report is a process gap, not a surprise
treating every flow-through as requiring a written agreement, even small foundation regrants
documenting each monitoring contact so the audit trail shows the oversight happened
reclassifying a relationship when the work changes — a contractor who starts doing program work has become a subrecipient

know_why.claim: Passing funds through to local organizations builds capacity where the work lives, and the pass-through entity's job is to monitor, not to do the work itself.
know_why.because: federal agencies and foundations fund intermediaries precisely because a local pass-through can reach and develop organizations the original funder cannot, and the written subaward plus scheduled monitoring is what makes the chain auditable under 2 CFR 200 Subpart D.
know_why.disputed_by: some program officers argue pass-through is risk-shifting — paying an intermediary to do what should have been funded directly — and that the subrecipient-monitoring burden becomes a bureaucratic tax on the small organizations it claims to build up.
know_why.source: 2 CFR 200 Subpart D (pass-through entity requirements) vs practitioner debate in the National Council of Nonprofits' regranting and subaward guidance

nodes.checkpoint: Draft a written subaward agreement for a real flow-through grant stating the subrecipient's scope, budget, period, reporting cadence, and audit duties, with a monitoring schedule of named due dates.
nodes.common_failure: Passing money without a written subaward and losing the audit trail; classifying a contractor as a subrecipient (or vice versa) and applying the wrong requirements; skipping subrecipient monitoring until the single audit finds it missing; failing to flow down the federal conditions the subaward inherits.
sources: 2 CFR 200 Subpart D — Post-Federal Award Requirements for Pass-Through Entities
National Council of Nonprofits — subaward and regranting guidance
Council on Foundations — regranting and donor-advised fund practice

nodes.label: Single audit readiness
nodes.one_line: Track federal expenditures to the $750,000 threshold and prepare the documentation a single audit will demand.
know_what: the $750,000 threshold (2 CFR 200.501) — a non-federal entity that expends $750,000 or more in federal awards in its fiscal year must have a single audit
the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (SEFA) — the required listing of every federal award with its Assistance Listing number and expenditures
Assistance Listing numbers (the former CFDA) — the catalog identifiers each federal program is reported under in the SEFA
major program determination — the risk-based selection of which federal programs the auditor tests in depth
2 CFR 200 Subpart F — the audit requirements, including auditor selection, the audit report, and corrective action
the audit findings and corrective action plan — the deficiencies the auditor reports and the pass-through or agency response they demand
subrecipient expenditure inclusion — a pass-through entity counts subaward expenditures in its own SEFA and federal-expenditure total
know_how: track federal expenditures by award and Assistance Listing continuously, reconciling to the general ledger at least quarterly
monitor cumulative federal spend against the $750,000 threshold so the audit obligation is known before year-end, not after
prepare the SEFA listing every federal award with its Assistance Listing number, direct and pass-through amounts, and total
identify major programs using the 2 CFR 200.518 risk criteria (Type A vs Type B thresholds) before the auditor does
assemble the award file — NOFO, notice of award, terms, amendments, and correspondence — for auditor access
coordinate with the chosen auditor on scope, timeline, and the compliance supplement for each program
draft a corrective action plan for any finding, addressing the root cause with named owners and dates
habits: tracking federal expenditures as a running number, not a year-end reconstruction
reconciling the SEFA to the general ledger before the auditor asks for it
keeping every award's Assistance Listing number in the award file from day one
treating the $750,000 threshold as a live risk to monitor, since one large award can cross it
preparing the corrective action plan before the audit closes, while the evidence is fresh
nodes.checkpoint: Prepare a Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards for your entity listing every federal award under its Assistance Listing number, and state whether total federal expenditures crossed the $750,000 single-audit threshold.
nodes.common_failure: Discovering the threshold was crossed at year-end with no expenditure documentation in place; filing a SEFA with wrong Assistance Listing numbers; forgetting that subaward dollars count in the pass-through entity's own total; treating the single audit as the auditor's problem until findings arrive.
sources: 2 CFR 200 Subpart F — Audit Requirements (single audit, $750,000 threshold)
OMB Compliance Supplement — program-specific audit guidance
AICPA — Single Audit Guide (Government Auditing Standards practice)
